result: IVIS imaging with CBA and Hspa1a promoters shows stable baseline expression patterns. The CBA promoter directs robust whole-body fLuc expression while Hspa1a::fLuc shows minimal luminescence primarily from liver, with both remaining stable from 30-68 days post-AAV delivery (C20-C22).
evaluation: Claims C20-C22 establish baseline expression patterns for control promoters using IVIS imaging. The data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrates expected differences between constitutive (CBA) and minimal (Hspa1a) promoters with appropriate temporal stability, providing validation for the imaging approach.

result: TREE sequences (REN and 2ankrd1aEN) direct injury-responsive transgene expression in mouse hearts after I/R injury. Both TREEs showed marked increases in cardiac bioluminescence that peaked within 3 days post-injury and returned to baseline by 35 dpi, with no change after sham surgery (C23-C25). However, off-target liver expression was observed for all AAV vectors including TREE-containing constructs (C26).
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 demonstrate injury-responsive TREE activity using longitudinal IVIS imaging. The temporal dynamics (peak at 3 dpi, return to baseline by 35 dpi) and injury-specificity (no change with sham) support the conclusion. However, sample size is very small (n=2 mice for I/R, n=3 for sham in C24-C25), which limits statistical power. The off-target liver expression (C26) is an important finding that motivates subsequent experiments.

result: AAV.cc84 eliminates off-target liver expression while maintaining cardiac transduction. AAV.cc84 showed no detectable liver signal over 35 days (C27) with substantially lower liver expression than AAV9 (C28), while cardiac luminescence remained similar between capsids (C29). This was confirmed by qPCR showing much higher AAV9 liver viral loads (C30) but similar cardiac loads (C31) between capsids (C32).
evaluation: Claims C27-C32 provide convergent evidence from IVIS imaging, ex vivo organ imaging, and qPCR that AAV.cc84 successfully detargets liver while maintaining cardiac tropism. The data includes appropriate sample sizes (n=6 for imaging, n=3 for qPCR) and multiple complementary measurements. Statistical comparisons are reported with specific p-values in figures.

result: Post-injury AAV.cc84 delivery of 2ankrd1aEN directs long-lasting, injury-responsive cardiac expression. When delivered at 4 dpi, 2ankrd1aEN-Hspa1a::fLuc showed robust cardiac activity that increased through 28 dpi and plateaued (C33), while Hspa1a alone remained minimal (C34). Expression was ~3-fold higher in I/R vs sham at 7 dpi (C35) and remained elevated throughout 63 days (C37), though sham mice also showed increasing baseline expression over time (C36), indicating long-lasting TREE-directed expression in injured hearts (C38).
evaluation: Claims C33-C38 demonstrate therapeutically relevant post-injury TREE delivery with appropriate controls and longitudinal tracking (n=4 mice per group). The data show both injury-responsiveness and durability of expression. The observation of increasing baseline in sham mice (C36) is appropriately noted and likely reflects AAV transduction kinetics rather than injury response. The conclusion about long-lasting expression (C38) is supported by the 63-day time course.

result: AAV capsid library screening identified AAV.IR41 with enhanced transduction of injured myocardium. Three capsids were enriched in infarcted vs remote tissue in I/R mice but not sham (C42). AAV.IR41 showed the highest reads and transduced I/R hearts more effectively than AAV9 and other variants (C43), with larger areas of transduction around infarcts (C44). Both AAV9 and IR41 primarily transduced cardiomyocytes at the border zone (C45-C46), identifying IR41 as having enhanced injured myocardium transduction (C47).
evaluation: Claims C42-C47 describe capsid screening and validation, but the screening used only n=2 I/R mice and n=1 sham mouse (C42), which is insufficient for robust identification of enriched variants. The validation experiments (C43-C46) lack sample size information and statistical analysis. While the approach is sound and the fluorescence imaging is compelling, the limited replication in the discovery phase and unclear validation statistics make the strength of this result uncertain.

result: AAV.IR41 shows enhanced cardiac transduction and TREE-driven expression compared to AAV9. IR41 delivered with 2ankrd1aEN-Hspa1a::fLuc showed higher expression in both sham and MI groups (C48), with significantly elevated cardiac radiance by 7 dpi that remained elevated at 21 dpi (C50). IR41 had ~2-fold higher cardiac viral uptake in MI mice (C51) and showed trends toward higher uptake in sham hearts (C52). The enhanced tropism of IR41 can complement injury-responsive TREEs for targeted cargo delivery (C53).
evaluation: Claims C48-C53 demonstrate enhanced performance of IR41 vs AAV9 with appropriate sample sizes (n=3-4 mice) and statistical testing showing significant differences at 7 and 21 dpi (C50). The qPCR data (C51) provides mechanistic support for the imaging observations. However, IR41 also showed higher hepatic expression (C49), which is a limitation. The conclusion (C53) appropriately integrates the findings about combining enhanced capsid tropism with injury-responsive enhancers.

result: IVIS imaging enables efficient, noninvasive assessment of TREE-directed transgene expression for developing enhancer-based cardiac gene therapies. The technique allows longitudinal tracking of expression amplitude and specificity (C54) and can assess effects of capsid and enhancer alterations to refine cardiac targeting (C55).
evaluation: Claims C54-C55 represent appropriate conclusions about the utility of the IVIS imaging approach based on the experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript. The work successfully shows longitudinal tracking of multiple TREE/capsid combinations with quantitative measurements, supporting these methodological conclusions.

result: IVIS imaging has limitations but revealed unexpected off-target TREE expression. Internal organ expression must be approximated with subjective ROIs that cannot be verified until sacrifice (C56), but this approach detected unexpected off-target TREE expression in liver, neck, and abdomen that was modulated by capsid engineering (C57).
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the IVIS technique while noting its utility in detecting off-target expression. The limitation about ROI subjectivity (C56) is a valid concern for internal organs, but the detection of off-target expression (C57) demonstrates the technique's practical value despite this limitation.

result: The study has several limitations requiring future work. Understanding IR41's enhanced tropism requires exploring cell surface markers/receptors and engineering liver detargeting (C58), potentially by combining AAV.cc84 and IR41 modifications (C59). IVIS imaging is not suited for larger animals due to tissue penetrance limitations (C60), mouse findings may not translate to larger models or humans (C61), and capsid screening was limited to mice (C62).
evaluation: Claims C58-C62 appropriately identify limitations and future directions. These are reasonable acknowledgments of the study's scope and the need for additional mechanistic work (C58-C59) and validation in other species (C60-C62). These represent standard limitations for mouse-based AAV studies.

result: This work establishes a foundation for refining TREE-targeted factor delivery to injured myocardium and expanding therapeutic tissue repair applications, though further optimization is required.
evaluation: Claim C63 is an appropriate summary conclusion based on the demonstrated ability to longitudinally track TREE expression, reduce off-target effects with AAV.cc84, and identify enhanced capsids like IR41. The acknowledgment that further optimization is required is appropriate given the identified limitations.

result: TREEs are injury-responsive regulatory elements that can direct transgene expression across species. TREEs direct expression in injured/regenerating tissues (C1) and zebrafish TREEs work in mammalian hearts after AAV delivery (C2). Originally described in zebrafish hearts (C11), TREEs have been identified across multiple tissues and species (C12-C13) and zebrafish TREEs are recognized by mammalian transcriptional machinery (C14). AAV-TREE vectors can spatiotemporally target injured hearts or spinal cord (C15), with examples like TREE-YAP stimulating cardiac recovery (C16), establishing TREEs as targeting vehicles for regenerative augmentation (C17).
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C11-C17 establish the background on TREEs based on prior published work (multiple citations provided). These claims appropriately summarize established knowledge from the field and provide context for the current study. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

result: Multiple genetic and environmental factors influence cardiomyocyte proliferation and regeneration after cardiac injury. Many genes affecting CM proliferation have been identified in zebrafish and mouse (C6), including mitogenic factors like Neuregulin1/ErbB signaling (C7), transcription factor Klf1 (C8), and Yap/Taz factors normally restrained by Hippo (C9). The signaling environment is complex with multiple cell types and factors influencing CM regeneration (C10).
evaluation: Claims C6-C10 provide appropriate background on cardiac regeneration biology based on extensive prior literature (multiple citations for each claim). These establish the scientific context and rationale for developing targeted delivery approaches like TREE-AAV vectors.

result: Engineered AAV capsids can modulate tissue tropism and cell-type specificity. New capsid variants have been developed including liver-detargeting AAV.cc84 (C18-C19), and directed evolution of AAV libraries has been used to discover capsids with improved properties like liver detargeting, enhanced potency, and cell-type tropism (C39).
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C39 establish background on AAV capsid engineering based on prior published work (citations provided). These provide context for the use of AAV.cc84 and the capsid library screening approach in the current study.

result: AAV9 preferentially transduces border zones of infarcted myocardium when delivered acutely after injury, potentially due to increased capillary permeability, sialidase activity, and DNA damage after cardiac ischemia.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 cite prior work (Konkalmatt et al., 2012) establishing AAV9's preferential border zone transduction. This provides rationale for the timing choice (9 dpi) in the capsid library screening to avoid acute injury effects. The mechanistic speculation (C41) is appropriately attributed to the cited work.

result: Detailed methodological procedures for I/R injury, AAV production, IVIS imaging, and other experimental techniques are described, including surgical procedures (C64-C67), capsid library construction (C68-C69), imaging protocols (C70-C72), experimental design decisions (C73-C75), capsid sequences (C76-C78), and other technical details (C79-C84).
evaluation: Claims C64-C84 describe methodological details that are appropriately documented. These include established procedures (I/R surgery adapted from Kaiser et al. 2005), standard techniques (AAV production, IVIS imaging), and specific experimental parameters. The methods appear sufficiently detailed for reproducibility, with appropriate citations to prior protocols and clear documentation of modifications.
